message:
feat(directory): speak https, and prove the two transports answer alike

The directory client refused https outright. That refusal is why the
observe-port defect could not even be reproduced through the real code
path: an https url stopped at the parser, several layers above the place
that computed 443 + 1 and sent the observation to 444.

The parser now accepts both schemes, defaults the port from the scheme
(80 / 443), and hands the answer back through outSecure. That is the only
place the question is asked. Whoever dials has to use the same answer the
parser used to pick the default port, and asking twice is how those come to
differ. All six callers take it from there.

The http branch was also matched case-sensitively while the https branch
was not, inside the same function -- so HTTP://host matched neither and
came out as "unsupported url scheme", a correctly typed url refused for its
capitals. One comparison now, for both.

https goes over WinHTTP, http stays on the socket that already works: no
existing deployment changes a byte. But two transports chosen by the url
means a difference between them is a defect visible on one kind of
deployment only -- and https is the one nobody can attach a debugger to. So
they are held against the same server, in-process on an ephemeral loopback
port, and compared on status, body, headers sent, and what each says when
there is no answer. That found two real differences:

  * Response limits were 64 KiB, 256 KiB and 4 MiB in three places, and all
    three answered an oversized response with a silently truncated one. The
    caller then reported malformed json -- true about what it was handed,
    false about the server. One limit now, and past it the exchange fails
    and says so.
  * On that refusal WinHTTP left a 200 in the status while the socket path
    left 0. A false return means the exchange did not happen; leaving a 200
    behind it invites code that checks the status without the return.

The bootstrap's https refusal, request.advertised (port and host), the
fallback when the advertised host is unusable, and the pin outranking the
advertisement are all asserted now -- through the real directory_session_open,
against .invalid names that cannot resolve, so what is checked is the
decision and not a network. The endpoint it decided on is visible because
the resolution error names it, which it did not before: "cannot resolve
directory host" sent whoever read it to look at the url, which may be the
one thing that is right.

The updater is untouched and gains a regression saying so. Sharing a
transport is not sharing a policy: it still refuses http at the entry point,
because what it fetches runs with administrator rights.

Not covered: certificate rejection and redirect downgrade. Both need a TLS
server, and the certificate for one is not this test's to create. The
posture is asserted by construction instead -- there is no parameter in the
transport that could switch validation off.
